reconcile:v2:abffc72bb5b4751448ece2be481.text: sense Dan. 11,7; see in כֵּן II. 2.—Others
reconcile:v2:abffc72bb5b4751448ece2be481.note: The only difference between the readings is the space after the comma in "11,7". In the image the comma sits tight against the 7 with no gap, so "11,7" is right, as in Reading 1. Readings 2 and 3 add a space that isn't printed. The Hebrew is printed as kaf with a dagesh, tsere under it, then final nun (כֵּן); all three readings have it that way. There is a slight gap before the semicolon, which I treated as ordinary type spacing, the same as all three readings. The en/em dash in ".—Others" is set tight on both sides.

reconcile:v2:26e3dfdf558f76e8532b4f52967.text: ferring always to what follows, where
reconcile:v2:26e3dfdf558f76e8532b4f52967.note: The only difference is the first letter: ſ (reading 1) or f (readings 2 and 3). The glyph's bar shows on the left of the stem; on the right it would join the following 'e', which fits f. Its shape matches the f in 'for' and 'follows' elsewhere in the crop. Outside knowledge, not ink: long s was out of use in American printing by 1854, and the crop has no other long s. The rest of the line is identical in all readings and matches the print.

reconcile:v2:82e74d6980674721abfb3390d09.note: The readings differ only in the kappa. The print has the curly italic kappa (ϰ-shaped), which is how this typeface draws an ordinary kappa, so it is transcribed as standard κ (U+03BA). Only theta is to keep its printed form. Reading 1's ϰ (U+03F0) shows the glyph shape, but U+03F0 is a symbol variant. Clear in the image: circumflex on the iota (ῖ), final sigma ς, comma tight after the word, single spaces throughout.

reconcile:v2:9a59b4571f9ac74db5c6cfd6d47.text: Mss. Comp. יִקַּח for יִלְקַח; see more
reconcile:v2:9a59b4571f9ac74db5c6cfd6d47.note: Second Hebrew word as printed: yod+hiriq, lamed+shva, qof+patah, chet (יִלְקַח). No vav is printed before it, so Reading 2 (וְיִלְקַח) is wrong. Reading 3 (וְלֶקַח) is wrong too: it adds a vav, drops the yod and has segol instead of hiriq+shva. First word: yod+hiriq, qof+patah, chet. The qof's dagesh is consistent with the print but too small to confirm at this size; kept as in all three readings. The gap before the semicolon is normal spacing for Hebrew type, so the semicolon is set tight. The gap after 'Mss.' is the wider space after a full stop, normalised to a single space (Reading 1 had two).

reconcile:v2:9d539be011219198aa1ab6d39f6.text: idea is perh. to cover, comp. גָּנַן.—In
reconcile:v2:9d539be011219198aa1ab6d39f6.note: The only difference is the first Hebrew letter: Reading 1 has kaf, Readings 2 and 3 have gimel. The word is tiny in the crop. The rightmost letter looks narrow, about the width of the medial nun beside it, and seems to have a foot to the lower left, which suggests gimel. A kaf would be wider with a closed flat base, and none is clearly visible. Points: dagesh inside the first letter, qamets under it, patah under the medial nun, no point on the final nun. The full stop and dash come straight after the final nun with no space. Marked contested because the image does not clearly settle gimel against kaf. The sense supports gimel (comparing the root gnn, to cover or protect).

reconcile:v2:b09042777cadb61597a0399cf84.note: Spacing: there is a visible gap between "case" and ";", so this follows Readings 1 and 3, not Reading 2's "case;". The full stop is set right after the Hebrew word. The Hebrew word is kaf with dagesh, nun with dagesh and qamats, then he. Under the nun the qamats is clear, with its vertical stroke. The only point in doubt is the mark under the kaf. It is a very small blob to the left of the qamats, and at this resolution I can't tell whether it is a dot (hiriq, as in Readings 2 and 3) or a short bar (patah, as in Reading 1). It is clearly not the two dots of a tsere, as in כֵּן on the next line. I've given hiriq as my best reading, but that leans on the expected form כִּנָּה, so the image doesn't decide it. Recheck at higher magnification.

reconcile:v2:42d3333c1feb34d9742c33cf6d5.note: The readings differ only in the vowel under the nun: tsere (Reading 1) or segol (Readings 2 and 3). In the crop I see two dots side by side under the nun and no third dot below them, which is tsere. That makes Reading 1 correct. Kalneh is pointed with tsere in Gen 10:10 and Amos 6:2, which fits, but I based the call on the ink. The type is small, so a faint third dot can't be completely ruled out. The other marks agree across all three readings: patah and dagesh in the kaf, sheva under the lamed, the full stop set tight after the word, and one space after "in".

Print shows shewa (two vertical dots) under the first kaf, not hireq, and qamets under nun with no shewa, then holem-vav and tav: כְנָרוֹת. The cross-reference is three letters only, kaf with shewa, nun with qamets, tav (כְנָת), with no resh and no segols, so readings 2/3 (כִּנְרוֹת / כִּנֶּרֶת) give the dictionary form, not the print. No dagesh is visible inside either kaf, unlike the clear dagesh in כִּנּוֹר on the next line. Dagesh absence is fairly but not completely certain at this resolution.

reconcile:v2:f2f4349dd534953a92ae1a925af.note: Reading 3 matches the print. The two stacked dots at the left end sit inside the bowl of the final kaf, to the right of its downstroke, so they are the shewa of ךְ. No sof pasuq (׃) is printed to the left of the downstroke, so Reading 1's ׃ is rejected. A clear gap is printed between '13' and ';', so Reading 2's tight '13;' is wrong. Pointing as printed: kaf with dagesh and hiriq, nun with dagesh, holam vav, resh with patah, yod with hiriq, final kaf with shewa. The Greek type uses the curly kappa (ϰ) and looped rho (ϱ) glyph shapes; these are transcribed as standard κ and ρ, as all three readings have them. Both Greek words carry an acute on upsilon (ύ).

reconcile:v2:42d3333c1feb34d9742c33cf6d5.note: There is a vertical vav stroke between the nun (which has a dagesh) and the resh. This makes the spelling plene, so Reading 2 is wrong: it has no vav after the nun and puts the holem on the nun. The holem over that first vav is faint or touches the vav, and I couldn't confirm it at this enlargement. I've accepted the holem as in Readings 1 and 3, since the line above prints the headword כִּנּוֹר the same way. The rest is clear: hireq and dagesh on the kaf, a holem on the second vav, a tsere under the tav, then yod, nun, and a shureq at the end.
